rules.title: Fatal processor hardware error
rules.meaning: The processor reported an error it could not recover from. This points to failing hardware, overheating, or unstable overclocking.
rules.action: Undo any overclocking, check that fans and vents are clean, and update the BIOS/UEFI. If it keeps happening, the CPU, RAM, or motherboard may need replacing.

rules.title: Corrected hardware error
rules.meaning: A hardware component (usually a PCIe device or the processor) had an error that was fixed automatically. A few are normal; many in a short time suggest a device is starting to fail.
rules.action: If this appears often, update the BIOS/UEFI and chipset drivers, and reseat or test recently added hardware.

rules.title: Corrected memory error
rules.meaning: The RAM returned bad data that was corrected automatically. Repeated errors are an early sign of failing memory.
rules.action: Run Windows Memory Diagnostic. If errors continue, reseat or replace the RAM sticks.

rules.title: Bad block on a drive
rules.meaning: Part of a drive can no longer be read reliably. Data on it is at risk.
rules.action: Back up your files now. Then check the drive's health (for example with CrystalDiskInfo or the maker's tool) and plan to replace it.

rules.title: Drive error during paging
rules.meaning: Windows hit an error while moving memory to or from a drive. This can mean a failing drive or a loose cable.
rules.action: Back up your files, check the drive's health, and reseat its cable if it's a desktop PC.

rules.title: Drive operation had to be retried
rules.meaning: A read or write to a drive took too long and had to be tried again. Occasional retries happen; many suggest a drive problem.
rules.action: Update the storage driver and drive firmware, and check the drive's health. Back up if retries are frequent.

rules.title: File system corruption detected
rules.meaning: The structure of the file system on a drive is damaged.
rules.action: Back up your files, then run 'chkdsk /f' on the affected drive from an administrator command prompt and restart.

rules.title: Display driver stopped responding and recovered
rules.meaning: The graphics driver froze and Windows restarted it. You may have seen the screen go black or flicker.
rules.action: Install the latest graphics driver from NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel. If it happens in games, check GPU temperatures and undo overclocking.

rules.title: App crashed
rules.meaning: These programs closed unexpectedly.
rules.action: Update or reinstall the app. Crashes in a graphics module such as d3d11.dll or a GPU driver file often go away after a graphics driver update.

rules.title: App stopped responding
rules.meaning: These programs froze and were closed.
rules.action: Update the app. If many different apps hang, check for a full disk, low memory, or a failing drive.

rules.title: .NET app crashed with an unhandled error
rules.meaning: A program built on .NET hit an error it didn't handle and closed.
rules.action: Update or reinstall the app, and install .NET updates through Windows Update.

rules.title: Service failed to start
rules.meaning: A background service didn't start, or took too long to start.
rules.action: If the service belongs to software you use, reinstall or update it. If it belongs to software you've removed, it's safe to ignore.

rules.title: Service stopped unexpectedly
rules.meaning: A background service crashed or stopped with an error.
rules.action: Update or reinstall the software the service belongs to. For Windows services, install updates and run 'sfc /scannow' from an administrator command prompt.

rules.title: Windows Update failed to install
rules.meaning: An update downloaded but could not be installed.
rules.action: Restart and run Windows Update again. If it keeps failing, run the Windows Update troubleshooter or search for the error code.

rules.title: PC ran low on memory
rules.meaning: Windows nearly ran out of memory, which makes apps slow, freeze, or crash.
rules.action: Close programs you aren't using, check Task Manager for one using far more memory than expected, and make sure the page file is enabled. Adding RAM helps if this happens often.

rules.title: A driver failed to load
rules.meaning: A device driver didn't load at startup, so the device may not work.
rules.action: Check Device Manager for devices with a warning icon and update their drivers. If everything works, this is usually harmless.

rules.title: A disk is nearly full
rules.meaning: A drive is at or near capacity, which can cause errors and slowdowns.
rules.action: Free up space with Disk Cleanup or Storage Sense, or move files elsewhere.

rules.title: Website name lookups timed out
rules.meaning: The PC couldn't look up some website names in time. Brief network drops cause this and it's usually harmless.
rules.action: If websites often fail to load, restart your router, or try a different DNS server.

rules.title: Processor speed was limited by the firmware
rules.meaning: The firmware slowed the processor down, usually because of heat or a power limit. The PC feels slow while this happens.
rules.action: Clean the vents and fans, make sure the PC is on a hard surface, and use the original charger on a laptop. Update the BIOS if the problem continues.

rules.title: PC went to sleep
rules.meaning: Windows put the PC to sleep (or into connected standby).

rules.title: PC woke from sleep
rules.meaning: The PC resumed from sleep.

rules.title: Planned restart or shutdown
rules.meaning: A program or person asked Windows to restart or shut down.

rules.title: DCOM permission warnings (harmless, safe to ignore)
rules.meaning: Windows components log these routinely. Microsoft says they don't affect how the PC works.

0x1A: often faulty RAM; run Windows Memory Diagnostic
0x3B: a driver or system file problem
0x50: a faulty driver, RAM, or antivirus
0x9F: a driver failed during sleep or wake
0xD1: a network, storage, or graphics driver crashed
0xEF: a core Windows process stopped; check the disk and system files
0x116: a graphics driver or GPU problem
0x124: a hardware fault: CPU, RAM, overheating, or overclocking
0x133: a driver or SSD firmware hung
0x139: a driver, RAM, or corrupt system files
